PullRequest.Title: Fix Enterprise Managed OTel Race in Copilot Extension
PullRequest.Body:
Enterprises use Managed Settings to configure OTel for Copilot chat sessions. Previously, an initialization race could leave the Copilot extension running with its original OTel configuration after the enterprise configuration arrived. In particular, export could remain off for the rest of the window even though Settings showed it enabled.

### Fix

Compare current OTel settings against the configuration used to construct the running service, both after activation and on OTel configuration changes. If a late enterprise configuration enables OTLP export that was initially off, show a progress notice and request an extension-host restart to rebuild the telemetry service with the managed configuration.

**Why restart the host?** Replacing just the OTel object would leave existing consumers, event subscriptions, and the embedded runtime using old state. In-process recovery is feasible, but needs a coordinated reinitialization path. For this Local-harness hotfix, we reuse the existing host-restart lifecycle and limit it to one automatic attempt per session.

Recognized enterprise OTel settings replace the whole personal OTel settings block, rather than merging with it. Fields omitted by the enterprise use defaults. Other settings are unaffected.

### Restart behavior

- **No managed OTel configuration:** no automatic restart. Personal settings edits and unrelated enterprise policies do not change the policy-backed OTel defaults used by this guard. An enterprise subscription alone is not sufficient.
- **Policy available at initialization:** no restart; the service already uses that configuration.
- **Policy arrives late:** at most one automatic recovery attempt per workspace/editor session. This will commonly be around startup, but can also follow a later sign-in.
- **Later policy changes or repeated refreshes:** no further automatic restart. Changed settings offer an opt-in reload; unchanged values do nothing. There is no polling or periodic restart.
- **Future launches:** a restart is not automatic on every launch. A new session can recover again only if the late-arrival case recurs.

An eligible restart affects other extensions in the window and can interrupt work. It is preceded by an auto-clearing progress notice and respects existing active-session shutdown vetoes. Successful recovery is logged without a confirmation toast. A failed or declined attempt falls back to a manual reload, not repeated automatic attempts.

### Accepted gaps and rationale

Telemetry produced before policy arrives and recovery completes is not guaranteed to be exported. This is not limited to a first-ever run, and we do not assume policy always arrives before the first chat request. Policies indistinguishable from schema defaults remain a limitation of using the existing configuration API.

Environment-variable precedence is unchanged: overrides remain an accepted risk. The `package.json` descriptions correct the documentation, not the behavior. Full enterprise-over-environment enforcement across the resolver, exporters, and embedded SDK is separate work.

This is a tactical fix for the Local harness while moving toward Agent Host. A proposed policy-inspection API would improve provenance but would not make policy arrive earlier or reconfigure an initialized service. Holding activation would require a readiness signal before OTel initialization and defined failure/timeout behavior without delaying unmanaged users. Those broader startup/API changes are deferred rather than added to this hotfix.

The comparison/fingerprint covers the resolved configuration and `github.copilot.chat.otel.{enabled,exporterType,protocol,otlpEndpoint,captureContent,serviceName,resourceAttributes,headers,outfile,maxAttributeSizeChars,dbSpanExporter.enabled}` defaults. The last two are tracked but are not policy signals.

### Manual Testing

<details>
<summary>Manual Test Steps</summary>

Use the [single-script macOS repro](https://gist.github.com/rwoll/10ca818de4a1e5b44d527d54914c7270), which combines a console collector and temporary managed-settings file. Requires macOS, Node.js 18+, and a free port 4318.

1. **Start without managed OTel.** Use a disposable test setup and an approved account with no existing OTel policy from the account or MDM. `/Library/Application Support/GitHubCopilot/managed-settings.json` must not exist; the script refuses to overwrite it. Close other VS Code windows because this policy is machine-wide. Leave personal OTel and DB export disabled and clear OTel environment overrides from the test launcher. A fresh profile alone does not isolate machine policy.

2. **Activate Copilot before applying policy.** Open the patched extension on Insiders (`--extensionDevelopmentPath /path/to/vscode/extensions/copilot`) or the local build (`./scripts/code.sh`). Sign in and select the **Local** harness, not Agent Host. Send a harmless request such as "Reply with OK" while OTel is still off, ensuring Copilot has activated.

3. **Run the gist in one terminal.** Download `otel-restart-test.cjs` and run:

   ```sh
   sudo node otel-restart-test.cjs
   ```

   The collector starts immediately. Press **Enter** only after step 2, then switch back to VS Code. The script deliberately waits **8 seconds** to make late policy arrival easy to observe; this is a test delay, not an estimate of production latency. It then prints `Test policy applied for 120 seconds.` and enables managed OTel pointing at the collector. The automatic extension-host restart is usually near-instant: you may only glimpse a brief progress notification, which dismisses automatically as the host restarts. No **Developer: Sync Account Policy** command is needed.

4. **Verify export.** Once Copilot chat is ready, send another harmless **Local** request and allow about 10 seconds for batching. The script's terminal should print `POST /v1/traces` and JSON data. There is no success toast; recovery is recorded in the Copilot output log. Use harmless prompts and review printed telemetry before sharing.

**Cleanup:** After 120 seconds, or on Ctrl+C, the script removes only its unchanged test file and stops the collector. Do not edit that file during the run. Policy withdrawal should offer a manual reload, not another automatic restart. Reload or close the test window afterward; use a fresh editor session to repeat the test.

**Before-fix comparison:** Repeat the same flow on an unpatched build. Policy becomes visible, but there is no automatic restart or new trace export until a manual reload.

**Additional controls:** Without enterprise OTel policy, personal settings edits should only offer a reload. To check settings replacement, repeat with personal service-name/resource-attribute values configured before the test; these must not appear in the printed managed telemetry.

This deliberately delivers policy after activation. The unit regression separately covers policy arriving between service construction and watcher registration.

</details>

Resolves #336102.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The before/after resolver behavior is explicit in the diff, the manifest confirms this key has no policy reference and defaults to 0, and numerous traced production call sites use this value to bound content attributes that the SDK retains and batch-exports. Exact payload sizes vary, but the loss of the bound and its scaling are deterministic.
Findings.PerformanceResource: Serialized prompt, response, tool, and hook attribute bytes retained by spans/batches and encoded into OTLP requests.
Findings.PerformanceScaling: Cost changes from at most the configured number of characters per content attribute to the full payload size, multiplied by the several content attributes and model/tool spans emitted during each agent turn; large contexts and tool results amplify retained and exported bytes.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Larger OTLP batches increase extension-host memory/GC pressure and network transfer, and can exceed collector attribute/request limits that the setting was intended to enforce.
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Service construction previously passed `otelSettings.get<number>('maxAttributeSizeChars')` directly to `resolveOTelConfig`, so an enterprise policy for enablement/endpoint/capture settings did not discard the user's positive content-size bound.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: The new resolver obtains `maxAttributeSizeChars` through `read()`. Whenever any recognizable enterprise OTel setting exists, `read()` returns `inspect().defaultValue` for every key; because `maxAttributeSizeChars` is not policy-backed, that value is the schema default `0` (unlimited), even when the user configured a positive cap.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: Added lines 79-82 switch all settings to policy/default values when `hasEnterpriseSettings` is true, and added line 91 routes `maxAttributeSizeChars` through that switch. The replaced code in `services.ts` read this key directly from effective user settings.
Findings.Title: Preserve the configured OTel attribute-size cap under policy
Findings.Impact: In an enterprise-managed OTel deployment, a user who configured a finite `maxAttributeSizeChars` limit silently gets unlimited attributes after this change. Large agent contexts or tool results are then retained and exported in full on each turn, increasing memory and network cost and risking oversized batch failures.
Findings.Evidence: `truncateForOTel` explicitly treats values <= 0 as unlimited. Chat/model/tool paths pass `config.maxAttributeSizeChars` when attaching serialized input messages, system instructions, tool definitions, request metadata, tool arguments, results, and outputs. `RealSpanHandle` keeps these strings in its attribute map, while `NodeOTelService` uses `BatchSpanProcessor` and OTLP exporters, so removing the cap increases retained and transmitted attribute bytes until each batch exports.
Findings.Recommendation: Keep user-only controls outside the enterprise block replacement: read `maxAttributeSizeChars` directly from `settings.get()` (while retaining the existing environment-variable precedence), and add a policy-present regression test that preserves a positive user cap.

Scenarios.Scenario: Copilot activation with no managed OTel configuration
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Service registration synchronously snapshots 13 OTel environment variables and resolves 11 cached VS Code settings before selecting the in-memory or real OTel service. OTelContrib schedules one additional drift check 500 ms after activation, off the activation critical path.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: A fixed 11-setting configuration block plus the cardinality of the headers/resourceAttributes maps; normally small and independent of workspace size.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Single synchronous initial resolution; the delayed check is scheduled once. Configuration-event checks are debounced and serialized by the monitor promise chain.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Environment values are snapshotted once. The active resolution is retained for comparison; each later check reads current cached configuration. No network cache is involved.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High confidence from service construction and contribution scheduling call paths.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Exact extension-API configuration-read cost is not measured, but work is fixed and small; no realistic startup regression was established.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression: disabled OTel still avoids loading the OTel SDK, and the added delayed fixed-size resolution is off the activation critical path.

Scenarios.Scenario: Late enterprise policy enables OTLP after Copilot activation
Scenarios.CriticalPath: After a configuration event and 500 ms debounce, the monitor resolves settings, persists a restart guard, then invokes the workbench extension-host restart command. Applying the policy depends on stopping and starting extension hosts; if the original host survives, a 15-second grace precedes the reload fallback.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Persist the one-shot policy restart record through VS Code workspaceState.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One write before an automatic restart and one acknowledgement write after a successful restart per editor session.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No restart guard was persisted because policy changes only prompted for a manual reload.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The first write must complete before requesting restart so a new host cannot loop; acknowledgement is startup follow-up and does not block normal feature use.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Execute the workbench extension-host restart command.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most one automatic command per workspace/editor session after a qualifying late policy arrival.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The extension displayed a reload prompt; it did not automatically restart extension hosts.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: This is the policy-recovery critical path and temporarily interrupts extension availability while hosts stop and reactivate.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Stop and restart the window's extension hosts.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One coordinated stop/start cycle for a qualifying late policy, guarded to one attempt per session.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No automatic host process cycle occurred on OTel policy arrival.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: All hosted extensions are unavailable during restart and then pay reactivation cost.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One policy transition; restart cost scales with the number and activation cost of extensions hosted in the window, not with the number of OTel settings.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Events are debounced and checks serialize. A workspace-state session record limits automatic restart to one attempt per editor session. The workbench command stops extension hosts as a coordinated operation before starting them.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The active pre-policy resolution is immutable. A workspace-state guard survives host restart and is acknowledged by the new host; warm repeated events with the same fingerprint do not restart again.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High confidence: the command implementation directly stops and starts extension hosts, and the session guard/debounce are explicit.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The number and activation cost of other installed extensions varies widely. The restart is nevertheless explicit, user-notified, one-shot, and central to the PR's stated recovery design, so it was treated as an intentional bounded tradeoff rather than a defect.
Scenarios.Verdict: No separate finding: the expensive restart is intentional, visible, and bounded to one attempt; no accidental loop, fan-out, or unbounded queue was found.

Scenarios.Scenario: Personal OTel edit or later managed-policy update
Scenarios.CriticalPath: An OTel-scoped configuration event schedules a 500 ms drift resolution. User changes and policy withdrawal/update compare against the activation snapshot and display a reload prompt; workbench reload occurs only if the user selects it.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Optionally execute Reload Window after explicit user selection.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Zero unless the user accepts the prompt; then one command per accepted prompt.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The prior watcher offered the same reload command for its six watched settings.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Not on the edit critical path unless accepted; reload behavior already existed before this PR.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: The fixed setting block and map sizes, at human configuration-edit frequency; rapid changes within 500 ms coalesce.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: RunOnceScheduler coalesces events, and monitor checks serialize. Same fingerprints are suppressed; established policy updates show at most one policy notice while stale.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The activation snapshot is retained; current settings are freshly resolved. The handled fingerprint suppresses unchanged repeated targets, with no negative-cache growth.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High confidence from the event filter, scheduler, monitor fingerprinting, and prompt path.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Map sizes are user/admin controlled, but realistic headers and resource attributes are small and checks occur only on OTel changes.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable repeated-work or boundary-fanout regression; the new watcher broadens coverage but remains debounced and event-driven.

Scenarios.Scenario: Agent turns after enterprise-managed OTel is active
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Model and tool paths serialize prompts, messages, tool definitions, arguments, results, and outputs into span/log attributes. Completed spans are retained by OTel batch processors and encoded for the configured OTLP exporter; exports are asynchronous but consume extension-host memory/CPU and network bytes.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Location: extensions/copilot/src/platform/otel/common/otelConfigResolution.ts:79-91 reaching messageFormatters.ts:24 and model/tool call sites
ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Serialize free-form model/tool content and truncate it according to maxAttributeSizeChars before retaining it as OTel attributes.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Several serialized content attributes per model/tool span and multiple spans per agent turn.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: A positive user maxAttributeSizeChars setting remained effective even when other OTel fields came from policy; the new whole-block read replaces it with default 0 (unlimited).
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Serialization occurs on request/tool processing paths; retaining and exporting occur through the OTel SDK. The PR changes the byte bound, not the number of attributes.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Batch and send span/log attributes to the configured OTLP collector.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Existing batched exports; request count is not necessarily increased, but bytes per batch now scale with full content instead of the user's per-attribute cap.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same exporter boundary existed, but explicit user caps bounded each content attribute before batching.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Export is asynchronous, but larger batches increase retained memory, encoding work, network transfer, and risk collector-size rejection.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Content bytes per attribute multiplied by several attributes and model/tool spans per agent turn. Large contexts, generated output, and tool results are the effective cardinality; the configured positive max previously bounded each retained/exported string.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Span production follows concurrent model/tool activity; SDK batch processors aggregate completed spans, so overlapping calls can retain multiple content payloads until export.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No content cache or deduplication applies. Each span owns its content attributes; batching groups network requests but does not reduce payload bytes.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: Very high confidence from the resolver branch, manifest default/policy metadata, truncation helper semantics, numerous content call sites, and batch exporter implementation.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Exact payload and turn sizes vary, and environment variable COPILOT_OTEL_MAX_ATTRIBUTE_SIZE_CHARS still overrides the setting. The deterministic loss of a configured finite bound under any recognized enterprise block is independent of that magnitude uncertainty.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reported: the diff deterministically converts a user-configured finite content bound to unlimited under enterprise policy, increasing retained and exported bytes with content size.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all 12 changed files and traced activation, configuration events, host restart/persistence, and OTel content export. One introduced serialization/network scaling regression was submitted: enterprise block replacement discards the user-only attribute-size cap. The automatic extension-host restart is expensive but explicitly one-shot, coalesced, guarded, and integral to the intended recovery behavior, so it was not reported separately.

Stats.CostNote: Copilot SDK reports nano-AI units and model billing multipliers; it does not provide a USD conversion.
